cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate concern: One of 52 target business corporations was excluded due to unavailable data, and the 2005-2012 panel of 51 corporations is unbalanced (351 of 408 potential corporation-years, ~14% missingness, plus 2 COSANPA observations excluded as Tukey outliers in the sanitation model) without missing-data diagnostics.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Serious concern: GEE estimation with an independent working correlation matrix lacks utility fixed effects, year fixed effects, or a quasi-experimental identification strategy to address non-random selection of municipalities and utilities into privatization or regulatory oversight, and conditions on potentially endogenous post-treatment cost variables (OPEX, CAPEXd, CAPEXr).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate: Captures corporate ownership (private vs. public mixed-capital), regulatory agency level (state/micro-regional vs. municipal/district vs. unregulated), and tariff-setting regime (rate-of-return, price/revenue-cap, municipal negotiation) within the framework of Laws 8.987/1995 and 11.445/2007, but relies on binary dummies from agency/corporate websites and an undocumented survey without explaining whether regulatory transitions across 2005-2012 were coded time-varyingly.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Tariff outcomes are derived from standardized SNIS administrative billing records deflated by IPCA, but governance and regulatory regime indicators were collected from current websites and an unspecified survey without clear longitudinal transition coding, and capital return (CAPEXr) required proxy construction due to unavailable regulatory asset return data.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Strong / Low concern: Water supply (Lwt), sanitation (Lst), and joint (Ljt) tariff levels are objectively and consistently operationalized from SNIS records as total annual billed revenue divided by annual billed volume (m3) in constant 2012 Reais, though realized average revenue per m3 partly reflects consumer distribution across tariff blocks in addition to statutory tariff schedules.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: No information / Moderate concern: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported, and both working correlation selection (via QIC) and outlier removal (Tukey rule on Lst) were data-driven, although full regression tables are transparently reported across all three outcomes and all three regulatory subsamples.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Serious concern: From 1,455 Brazilian water and sanitation utilities, the sample is restricted exclusively to 51 of 52 business corporations (22 private and 30 mixed-capital corporations), excluding 934 directed public administrations, 416 municipal utilities, 5 public companies, and 39 private limited liability companies due to information availability.

domain_ratings.justification: Although the GEE regressions control for regional dummies, municipal GDP per capita, operational and capital expenditure metrics, tariff block structure, metering, water/sewage quality compliance, and number of locations served, the study employs no quasi-experimental design (such as difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, or firm and year fixed effects) to address endogenous selection into private concessions or state/municipal regulation. Using an independent working correlation matrix without unit fixed effects relies heavily on cross-sectional comparisons, and conditioning on contemporaneous unit costs (OPEX, CAPEXd, CAPEXr) risks controlling for post-governance mediators.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-7, Sections 4.1-4.2; PDF Pages 11-12, Appendix 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domain_ratings.justification: Out of 1,455 Brazilian water and sanitation utilities documented in Table 1, the authors restrict eligibility strictly to the 52 utilities organized as business corporations, explicitly excluding public companies, directed public administrations, municipal departments, and 39 private limited liability companies because of data availability. While business corporations cover roughly 73-74% of the served population, excluding non-corporate municipal utilities and smaller private LLCs introduces substantial selection bias when evaluating public versus private management and municipal negotiation versus agency regulation.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 2, Section 2.1 (Table 1); PDF Page 4, Section 4

domain_ratings.justification: Governance exposures (Priv, RRegA, LRegA, Rrat, Rcap) are operationalized as binary dummies sourced from SNIS, normative constitutions, agency and utility websites, and an unelaborated survey (Appendix 1). Because regulatory agencies expanded from 11 to 50 over the preceding decade (PDF Page 1) while regulatory characteristics were extracted from websites/surveys at the time of research, the paper does not establish whether exact dates of agency creation, contract delegation, or tariff-regime adoption between 2005 and 2012 were coded longitudinally, creating potential retroactive misclassification.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 1, Section 1; PDF Pages 4-5, Sections 4 and 4.1; PDF Page 11, Appendix 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domain_ratings.justification: In this observational comparison of statutory governance regimes, formal submission to a regulatory agency did not uniformly translate into active economic tariff regulation: the authors note that some utilities are supervised by regulatory agencies lacking a defined tariff system (PDF Page 5) and that some state agencies regulate services in cities without proper municipal authorization (PDF Page 10).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 3, Section 2.2; PDF Page 5, Section 4.1; PDF Page 10, Section 5.4

domain_ratings.justification: One of the 52 business corporations had no available data and was omitted, and the remaining 51 corporations over the 8-year window (2005-2012; 408 potential corporation-years) yield an unbalanced panel of 351 observations (~14% missingness), with 2 further observations (COSANPA in 2007 and 2011) dropped as Tukey outliers in the sanitation model (N = 349). No diagnostics are provided on why panel years are missing or whether missingness correlates with ownership, regulation, or tariff levels.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 4, Section 4; PDF Page 7, Section 4.2; PDF Page 8, Table 4

domain_ratings.justification: Tariff levels for water supply (Lwt), sanitation (Lst), and joint services (Ljt) are computed uniformly from standardized national SNIS billing data as total annual billed revenue divided by total annual billed cubic meters, deflated to 2012 price levels via the official IPCA index. While average revenue per billed cubic meter blends statutory tariff rates with consumer distribution across consumption blocks, measurement is objective and administrative across all comparator groups.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4 and 6, Section 4.1; PDF Page 11, Appendix 1

domain_ratings.domain_name: Bias in selection of the reported result
domain_ratings.justification: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan exists to verify whether covariate selection, subsample splits (overall, regulated, unregulated), QIC-based working correlation selection, and Tukey outlier exclusion were pre-specified. However, the authors transparently report full estimates for all three outcome definitions and all three subsamples.

overall_narrative_summary: Barbosa and Brusca (2015) conduct a comparative longitudinal panel evaluation (2005-2012; 51 utilities; N = 351 corporation-years) of how private versus public corporate management, regional/local regulatory agency oversight versus non-regulation, and rate-of-return or price/revenue-cap regimes versus municipal negotiation affect water and sanitation tariff levels in Brazil. Appraised under ROBINS-I, the overall risk of bias is Serious. The primary methodological vulnerabilities are confounding (D1: Serious) and participant selection (D2: Serious): the GEE specification with an independent working correlation matrix omits firm and year fixed effects, employs no quasi-experimental design to address endogenous sorting into privatization or regulation, conditions on potentially endogenous operational and capital costs, and restricts the sample exclusively to business corporations while omitting 1,403 non-corporate municipal, public, and private LLC utilities due to data availability. Moderate concerns also arise from potential retroactive website/survey classification of time-varying regulatory regimes (D3), partial implementation/unauthorized regulation in practice (D4), and ~14% unexplained panel missingness (D5), whereas administrative tariff outcome measurement via SNIS is objective (D6: Low) and no pre-analysis plan is available to assess selective reporting (D7: No information).
study_design_identified: Comparative longitudinal unbalanced panel econometric study (51 Brazilian water and sanitation utility business corporations over 2005-2012, N = 351 utility-years) using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE)

why_tool_chosen: The study is a non-randomized comparative longitudinal panel evaluation estimating the impact of utility governance and regulatory policy regimes (private vs. public management; state/regional vs. local regulatory agencies vs. unregulated; rate-of-return and price/revenue-cap regimes vs. municipal tariff negotiation) across genuine comparator groups over 2005-2012, which maps directly to ROBINS-I per RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1.
